title: Three Indian Sailors Are Dead After U.S. Navy Strikes. Delhi Has Summoned the American Envoy Twice.
excerpt: The Settebello strike killed three merchant mariners from UP, Himachal and Andhra. India is furious. Washington says comply or face consequences.
body:
Three Indian Seafarers Are Dead. India Has Summoned the American Envoy Twice. And Neither Side Is Backing Down.

Sushila Devi sat sobbing on the floor of her house in Deoria, Uttar Pradesh, after authorities confirmed that her husband Shivanand Chaurasia was one of three Indian sailors killed when a U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions into the engine room of the Palau-flagged tanker *Settebello* off the coast of Oman on Wednesday.

"If he had told us about the dangers, I would have called him back," she cried, surrounded by women from the family. "The government should not allow people to go there."

Chaurasia, the sole earner for a family with two young children, was among 24 Indian mariners aboard the Settebello when it was hit. Twenty-one were rescued after jumping overboard. The three missing sailors — from Himachal Pradesh, Deoria in Uttar Pradesh, and Andhra Pradesh — were found dead the following day.

## Three Ships, One Week, Zero Apologies

The Settebello was not the only vessel struck. The U.S. Navy hit three Indian-crewed tankers in a single week as part of its blockade of Iranian oil shipments. On Monday, the Marivex was disabled with precision munitions. On Thursday, two Hellfire missiles tore into the engine room of the *Jalveer* after its crew "repeatedly failed to comply" with American directions, U.S. Central Command said. All 20 Indian crew aboard were evacuated safely.

Since the blockade began on April 13, CENTCOM says it has disabled nine non-compliant vessels, redirected 135 others, and allowed 42 humanitarian aid ships to pass. But the escalation to lethal force — killing civilians on commercial ships — has crossed a line that India is not prepared to absorb quietly.

## Summoned Twice, Still Talking Past Each Other

India summoned the U.S. chargé d'affaires, Jason Meeks, twice in the span of days — a rare diplomatic escalation for a country that prizes continuity in its American relationship. The Ministry of External Affairs said it conveyed "deep concern over the use of lethal and deadly force against civilian shipping" and called the strikes "unacceptable."

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar spoke directly to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, reiterating India's "strong protest" over the deaths.

Washington's response was blunt and unapologetic. The State Department readout stressed that "all commercial vessels should immediately comply with orders from U.S. forces" and that "violations of the U.S. blockade and the illicit transport of Iranian oil will not be tolerated." There was no expression of regret over the Indian deaths.

## A Conflict India Did Not Start — But Is Paying For

India is the world's second-largest supplier of seafarers after the Philippines. Its sailors crew tankers, cargo ships, and bulk carriers across some of the most dangerous maritime corridors on earth. The Iran war, which began on February 28 with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes, has turned the Strait of Hormuz — which carried a fifth of the world's oil and LNG before the conflict — into a militarised chokepoint.

The Forward Seamen's Union of India warned that repeated attacks could deter workers from taking up seafaring jobs, worsening an already tight global labour market for merchant mariners. "The repeated incidents demonstrate the alarming deterioration of safety and security in one of the world's most important maritime corridors," said General Secretary Manoj Yadav.

## The Political Pressure Is Building

The opposition Aam Aadmi Party urged Prime Minister Modi to raise the issue directly with President Trump when the two leaders meet at the G7 summit in Évian next week. The Congress party accused the government's policies of having "emboldened external powers to act against Indian interests with impunity."

Strategic analyst Brahma Chellaney put it more sharply: "Had the victims been Chinese sailors instead, Beijing would almost certainly have reacted very differently, treating the strikes as a direct and lethal provocation."

Trump, for his part, accused Iran of launching a drone attack on Indian ships exiting the Strait — a claim he made without specifying which vessels — and called it "totally unacceptable." Iran's foreign ministry condemned the U.S. strikes on Indian-crewed ships, calling Washington's actions "armed robbery and state piracy."

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

For NRIs, the crisis touches a nerve that goes beyond geopolitics. Indian seafarers are overwhelmingly from middle-class and lower-middle-class families in states like Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Maharashtra, and Andhra Pradesh. Many are the sole breadwinners, sending remittances home to fund children's education and family expenses. The maritime industry is one of India's largest sources of foreign remittances, and any sustained threat to seafarer safety could ripple through household economies in dozens of districts.

The Modi-Trump bilateral at the G7 — now confirmed for Wednesday — will be their first face-to-face meeting since the India-Pakistan conflict. The killed sailors, the Strait of Hormuz, trade tariffs, and H-1B visas are all on the table. What India gets — or fails to get — will be closely watched by a diaspora that has skin in every one of those conversations.
